title: Why Nobody Leaves the Smoky Room
structure: claim hook, second-person scenario (Imagine), question, late explainer, last line is the sting of the explanation
fact: Latané and Darley (1968) put male Columbia University students in a waiting room to fill out a questionnaire and let smoke in through a wall vent. Alone, 75 % reported the smoke within the six-minute session; next to two actors who had been told to ignore it, 10 % did; in groups of three real participants, someone reported it in only 38 % of the groups. The authors' reading: people take other people's calm as a sign that nothing is wrong. DRAMATISED for this story: what 'you' think and do in the room, the stinging eyes, the clipboard, and how thick the smoke is at minute six.

sentences.text: Smoke poured into the room, and nine out of ten people just kept filling out a form.
Imagine you're in a waiting room with two strangers, ticking boxes on a survey.
Then a thin white wisp curls out of a vent in the wall.
You look up.
The guy on your left glances at it, shrugs, and goes back to his survey.
The guy on your right doesn't even blink.
So you figure it's probably steam, and you tick another box.
A minute later, that wisp is a cloud.
Your eyes sting, and you're waving your clipboard like you're landing a plane.
But they're both still writing, so you cough as politely as you can and keep going.
You almost stand up, but what if you're the only one making a fuss?
By minute six, you can barely see the door, and nobody has said a word.
So why is nobody running?
Well, this was a real experiment, and those two strangers were actors, told to ignore the smoke no matter what.
When students sat in that room alone, three out of four got up and reported it.
But next to two calm faces, only one in ten did.
You see, when you're not sure what's happening, you don't trust your own eyes.
You check everybody else's face instead.
So the researchers took the actors out and filled the room with three real people.
And most of those rooms sat in the smoke too, each of them waiting for somebody else to look scared first.
